extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, congressional staff, PTO stakeholders, patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and substantive criteria embedded in Senate debate and amendments to S.23 (America Invents Act) concerning PTO funding reform (lockbox/fee access/fee-setting) and a statutory exclusion of patents on tax strategies, including scope, exceptions, and implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockbox / revolving fund for PTO user fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a lockbox--a new revolving fund at the Treasury--where user fees that are paid to the PTO for a patent or a trademark go directly into the revolving fund for PTO to use to cover its operating expenses. Congress would not have the ability to take those fees and divert them to other general revenue purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to prevent fee diversion so PTO can reliably access user fees to cover operating expenses. Rationale offered: fee diversion has contributed to backlog and pendency problems; permanent end to fee diversion is necessary for efficient PTO operations. Examples of past diversion amounts and effects are cited to justify the lockbox. The amendment does not remove congressional oversight; it couples the lockbox with reporting and audit requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO fee-setting authority conditional on cost-recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 9: the PTO shall have authority to set or adjust any fee established or charged by the office provided that the fee amounts are set to recover the estimated cost to the PTO for its activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: fee-setting authority is meaningful only if PTO also has access to collected fees; otherwise raising fees risks Congress diverting them. The testimony and debate argue fee-setting plus guaranteed access to fees are both needed for a sustainable funding model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainable funding model requirements (President’s budget)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sustainable funding model includes: (1) ensuring access to fee collections to support the agency’s objectives; [and] (2) instituting an interim patent fee increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two elements are presented as immediate priorities to allow the agency to manage fluctuations in filings and revenues and sustain operations on a multi-year basis. The interim fee increase is specifically mentioned as part of near-term stabilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and transparency requirements for PTO access to fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment requires four different methods by which Congress will hold PTO accountable: (1) an annual report, (2) an annual spending plan to be submitted to the Appropriations Committees of both Houses, (3) an independent audit, and (4) an annual budget to be submitted to the President each year during the budget cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amendment asserts these reporting/audit/budgeting requirements will provide 'extensive transparency and accountability' and preserve the jurisdiction of congressional committees (Appropriations and Judiciary) to demand information and conduct oversight. The reporting requirements may yield more information to Congress than provided by other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent end to fee diversion as remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to permanently end fee diversion is the only effective remedy; the PTO must be able to permanently and consistently access the user fees it collects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: temporary restraint by appropriators does not guard against future diversion; past patterns and cumulative diverted amounts (cited figures since 1992) make a permanent solution necessary. The amendment is framed as necessary to enable PTO to budget and implement reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance objective: reduce backlog and pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent reform and stable funding should address two major PTO problems: (1) the growing number of unexamined patent applications (the backlog), and (2) the increased time it takes to have a patent application examined (pendency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmarks mentioned in debate: patent first action pendency ~26 months; total pendency ~35 months; total pending applications >1.16 million; over 718,000 waiting for first action. The guidance links access to fees and stable funding to the ability to hire examiners, reduce backlog, and shorten pendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 14 tax-strategy patent exclusion (core rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deterring tax liability ... will be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art for purposes of evaluating an invention under section 102 or under section 103 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: patents cannot be granted that give an exclusive right to utilize a tax strategy; the ability to interpret tax law and implement such interpretations remains in the public domain. This is presented as ensuring equal access to tax strategies and preserving fairness and uniform application of tax law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'tax liability' definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'tax liability' refers to any liability for a tax under any Federal, State, or local law, or law of any foreign jurisdiction, including any statute, rule, regulation, or ordinance that levies, imposes, or assesses such tax liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad definition is intended to capture strategies that affect liability under any governmental taxing authority, not limited to federal income tax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions especially suitable for tax-favored structures included
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions subject to this provision would include, for example, those especially suitable for use with tax-favored structures that must meet certain requirements, such as employee benefit plans, deferred compensation arrangements, tax-exempt organizations, or any other entities or transactions that must be structured or operated in a particular manner to obtain certain tax consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies whether the invention aids in satisfying qualification requirements for tax-favored status, takes advantage of specific tax benefits, or allows tax reduction/avoidance/deferral not otherwise automatically available. Examples: structured financial instruments or arrangements whose utility is inseparable from the tax benefit are within scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separable-claims rule (claims encompassing tax strategies vs. non-tax claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim that encompasses a tax strategy will be subject to the provision and the novelty or nonobviousness of the tax strategy will be deemed insufficient to differentiate that claim from the prior art. However, any other claim that does not involve a tax strategy would not be subject to the provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application contains multiple claims, only those claims that 'encompass' the tax strategy are barred by the provision; separable, non-tax-related claims may still be evaluated and, if otherwise patentable, enforced. The assessment of separability determines which claims are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implementation does not exempt tax strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that any computations necessary to implement an invention that is a strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability are done on a computer, or that the invention is claimed as computer implemented, does not exclude the strategy from the provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are separable from the tax strategy, the nontax claims are evaluated under sections 102 and 103 normally; but computer implementation by itself does not avoid the tax-strategy exclusion for claims that embody the tax strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for tax return preparation software (amendment/modification)
rubrics_metrics.description: This section does not apply to that part of an invention that is a method, apparatus, computer program product, or system, that is used solely for preparing a tax or information return or other tax filing, including one that records, transmits, transfers, or organizes data related to such filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that software/systems used solely for preparing/filing tax returns remain eligible for patent protection to the extent otherwise patentable, and such patents could not preclude others from implementing any tax strategy. This is a negotiated carve-out to the tax-strategy exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-intent to affect patents unrelated to tax strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision is not intended to deny patent protection for inventions that do not comprise or include a business method (e.g., a process to distill ethanol) merely because implementation may incidentally yield tax credits or reduced excise taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements clarify scope: inventions whose primary subject is not a tax strategy, and whose patentability does not rest on a tax consequence, are not intended to be barred. No inference is made about other areas of law (e.g., copyright vs. patent for software).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO consultation with Treasury/IRS to identify tax strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office may seek advice and assistance from Treasury and the IRS to better recognize tax strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: consultation should help ensure that patents do not infringe on the ability of others to interpret the tax law and that implementing such interpretations remains in the public domain. Practical implementation suggests interagency coordination to identify and adjudicate tax-strategy claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical outcome: equal access; no exclusivity over tax strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical result of this provision is that no one can be granted an exclusive right to utilize a tax strategy. The provision is intended to provide equal access to tax strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing of policy goal: preserve fairness and uniform application of tax law; avoid placing taxpayers in position of paying royalties or foregoing tax benefits. Emphasized as preserving taxpayer rights and avoiding added complexity (patent searches, infringement exposure) for tax advice.
